title: Growing the next generation of student leaders
description: A practical guide for Kenyan school principals on identifying, training, and supporting the next cohort of prefects and student leaders before the current leadership graduates.
body:
As Grade 12 prepares to leave, most Kenyan schools face an annual leadership transition — prefects, student council members, and club leaders who built trust and effectiveness over their tenure are replaced by a new cohort who must build that credibility from scratch. Schools that plan this transition deliberately maintain continuity in student leadership quality. Schools that leave it to chance often experience a leadership gap that affects school culture for a term or more.

Start identifying future leaders before the transition, not after

Waiting until Grade 12 has left to identify the next cohort of leaders means starting from zero. Schools that observe and informally mentor promising Grade 10 and 11 students throughout the year — noting who demonstrates responsibility, peer respect, and initiative — enter the formal selection process with a much clearer sense of genuine candidates, rather than relying solely on a popularity-based election or a brief interview process.

Build a genuine selection process, not just popularity

Purely popularity-based prefect selection sometimes elevates students who are well-liked socially but lack the maturity or consistency the role requires. A selection process that combines peer input, teacher observation, and a structured interview or written reflection component gives a more complete picture of a candidate's readiness for responsibility.

Practical approach: A shadowing period — where incoming leaders work alongside outgoing ones for the final few weeks of the outgoing cohort's tenure — transfers practical knowledge and relationship credibility that no amount of formal training alone can replicate.

Provide genuine training, not just appointment

Appointing a student to a leadership position without providing training in what the role actually requires — conflict resolution, communication, handling peer pressure from friends who expect favouritism — sets new leaders up to struggle unnecessarily. A structured orientation programme, even a single half-day session, covering practical scenarios new leaders will face significantly improves their early effectiveness.

Give leaders genuine authority and responsibility

Student leaders who are given only symbolic responsibility — wearing a badge but with no real decision-making role — quickly disengage from the position. Leaders who are given genuine responsibility, consulted meaningfully by the administration, and see their input lead to real outcomes take the role far more seriously, and this seriousness extends to how they are perceived and respected by their peers.

Support leaders through the challenges of the role

Student leadership, particularly prefect roles that involve enforcing rules among peers, carries genuine social difficulty — navigating friendships while maintaining fairness, managing peer pressure to look the other way on rule violations. Regular check-ins between the deputy principal and student leaders, specifically addressing these challenges, support leaders through difficulties that would otherwise cause them to either withdraw from the role or compromise their integrity in it.

Recognise outgoing leaders' contribution

A genuine, specific acknowledgement of outgoing student leaders' contribution — not just a certificate, but a recognition that names what they actually achieved — reinforces that leadership is valued by the school and encourages future students to aspire to it.
